USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Proceed with the already-committed Section 301 tariff package (~$50B at 25%) as the lever we have publicly staked our credibility on, but do not broaden it to the threatened $100B+ tranche or add new entity-list actions. Keep the negotiated channel open (Ross-Liu talks) and resist the temptation to expand, because China has explicitly tied its increased-purchase offers to the US not imposing further tariffs. Hold at the committed posture, impose as planned mid-June, and re-engage Beijing without new escalatory commitments.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat is moderate, not existential. The US is the initiating party and holds leverage: the Section 301 investigation produced findings (March 22, 2018) of unreasonable/discriminatory forced technology-transfer practices, and the US economy is demonstrably strong going into this — industrial production rose (INDPRO 101.5 in Jan to 103.2 in May/June), consumer sentiment ~98, and the broad dollar strengthened to ~112 (up from ~108), showing no material GDP drag yet. The material risk is China's threatened retaliation on ~$50B of US goods, which deliberately targets soybeans, corn, autos and aircraft — i.e., the farm belt that is the president's political base ahead of the November midterms (China's retaliation hit roughly $16.5B of ag/food and ~57% of US soybean exports go to China). That political-exposure factor, plus the G7 allies' 'unanimous concern' over the steel/aluminum tariffs, is what keeps this above neutral. But because the US is on the offensive with a strong economy and China's own package is contingent on us not escalating further, the situation still reads as manageably in our favor — hence +0.35 rather than +0.5. On action: escalating to the $100B+ level (which Trump floated on April 5) or forcing export controls would invite symmetrical retaliation directly against our farm exports and undercut the leverage we want to preserve in negotiation; conceding (dropping the tariffs) would void the only pressure we have and hand China a win. The disciplined move is to hold at the committed $50B level, impose as scheduled, and use the standing threat of further action to extract concessions in continuing talks. This aligns a mildly negative action_score (maintain the committed escalation rather than expand or retreat) with the moderate threat reading.
key_factors: Section 301 findings (Mar 22) on China's forced tech transfer justify US action and give US the initiative
US economy strong: INDPRO up to ~103, consumer sentiment ~98, broad dollar to ~112 — no material GDP drag yet
China retaliation (~$50B) targets soybeans/autos/aircraft, hitting the farm belt — Trump's political base before midterms
China's increased-purchase offer is explicitly conditional on US NOT imposing further tariffs
G7 allies voiced unanimous concern over US steel/aluminum tariffs
May truce collapsed May 29; US due to publish/impose 25% tariff list by mid-June

sources_cited.excerpt: USTR releases Section 301 report finding China's IP/tech-transfer practices unreasonable or discriminatory.
USTR publishes proposed Section 301 tariff list: ~1,300 Chinese product lines (~$50B).
China announces proposed retaliatory tariffs on ~$50B of US goods (incl. soybeans, automobiles, aircraft).
White House announces US will proceed with Section 301 actions, incl. 25% tariffs on ~$50B of Chinese imports. Truce collapses.
US industrial production 101.5 (Jan) to 103.2 (May/June), still growing.
China's retaliation hits ~$16.5B of US ag/food; soybeans account for ~57% of US soybean exports.
White House to publish final tariff list by Jun 15 and impose shortly after; China warns all trade outcomes void if US imposes tariffs.
